title: Cybersecurity
tagline: Protect your accounts, spot scams and react to an attack, all the way to the cybercafé workshop.

lesson.p: Your password is the key to your digital life: WhatsApp, Facebook, Mobile Money, e-mail. If someone guesses it, they act in your name.
Long (12 characters or more), with letters, numbers and symbols, and above all unique for each account. An easy-to-remember sentence works very well.
Your first name, your birth date, 123456, “password”, your phone number. These are a hacker's first guesses.
If you reuse the same one, a single leak opens all your accounts. Keep them in a password manager or a well-hidden notebook, never in a note anyone can see.

exercises.hint: Long, mixed, not a common word.
exercises.why: The longer and more mixed, the harder to guess.

exercises.q: Why avoid your birth date as a password?
options: It is easy to guess or find on your profiles

exercises.q: You use the same password everywhere. What is the risk?
options: One single leak opens all your accounts
exercises.why: If one site is hacked, attackers try that password elsewhere.

exercises.q: A good password should have at least how many characters? (number)
exercises.why: 12 characters or more is a good minimum.

exercises.q: Where should you keep your passwords?
options: In a manager or a well-hidden notebook
In a photo in your gallery
On paper stuck to the screen
exercises.why: A private place protects your passwords.

exercises.q: Put these in order to create a good password.
lines: Use it for this account only

lesson.p: A fake message (SMS, WhatsApp, e-mail) pretending to be a bank, operator or friend to make you click a fake link or give away your codes.
Urgency (“your account will be closed”), an offer too good to be true (prize, gift), mistakes, a strange link, a request for a code or password.
A code received by SMS (WhatsApp, Mobile Money) is to log YOU in. No serious company asks for it. If you give it, that person takes over your account.

lesson.h: What to do with a suspicious message
lesson.p: Don't click, don't reply. Check another way (call the person or the service). Delete and report the message.

exercises.q: A text says: “Your Mobile Money account will be closed, click here”. What do you do?
options: I don't click and I check with the official service
I send my code to prove it's me
I forward it to all my friends
exercises.why: Scammers create panic to make you act without thinking.

exercises.q: Which is a typical sign of a scam?
options: A prize you never asked for
A message from your usual friend in their usual words
A reminder of a planned appointment
exercises.why: A fake prize lures your data or money.

exercises.q: Someone asks for the code you got by SMS. What do you do?
options: I give it if the person is nice
I give it to a fake agent
exercises.why: Giving that code hands over the keys to your account.

exercises.q: What is the fake message that imitates a service to steal your info called? (one word: p…)
Put these in order for a suspicious message.
exercises.why: Don't click, verify, then delete and report.

exercises.q: Connect each danger to its right reaction.
exercises.why: Fake link: don't click. A code: don't give it.

lesson.p: On top of the password, a code sent to your phone confirms it is you. Turn it on for WhatsApp, Facebook, Google: a hacker with your password still can't get in.
Regularly check the list of devices connected to your account. If you see an unknown device, log it out and change your password.
On a public PC, always log out at the end and don't let the browser save your password. Avoid payments on an unknown Wi-Fi.
Updates fix security holes. Back up your photos and important documents: even after an attack, you don't lose everything.

options: It blocks a hacker who has your password
exercises.why: Even with your password, they lack the code on your phone.

exercises.q: You see an unknown device connected to your account. What do you do?
options: I log it out and change my password
exercises.hint: Cut access then change the key.
exercises.why: Logging it out and changing the password takes back control.

exercises.q: In a cybercafé, at the end of your session you must…
options: Log out of all your accounts
Save your password in the browser
Leave a paper with your code
exercises.hint: The next customer sits down after you.
exercises.why: Otherwise the next user can enter your accounts.

exercises.q: For two-step verification, how many proofs are needed in total? (number)

exercises.why: Updates close the doors attackers use.

exercises.q: Put these in order after an account hack.
exercises.why: Take the account back, lock it, then warn.

lesson.p: You are the security person of a cybercafé. 8 customers reported a problem. 4 are real threats, 4 are harmless. It's up to you to tell them apart.
For each customer: read the message, check the link or sender, look at the account activity and the password. Then pick the right protection.
Clicking to check or sending your code to prove your identity makes everything worse. Find the real threat first.

exercises.q: 4 customers are in danger (in red). Tap a customer, run the checks, then protect their account.
exercises.hint: Compare the message, the link, the activity and the password.
exercises.why: Four threats: fake link, weak password, hijacked account, code request.
cmds: Check the link or the sender

ok: Normal message from a known friend, nothing odd asked.
Usual logins, from their own phone.
weak: No odd login, but an attacker could try.
hijack: His contacts get money requests he didn't send.
Login from an unknown device far away.
otp: An “agent” writes: “Send me the code you got by SMS to confirm your account.”
Unknown number claiming to be customer service.
A blocked login attempt, waiting for the code.

repairs.label: Don't click, delete and report the message
Log out unknown devices and turn on two-step verification
Never give the code and block the number
Send the code to prove identity
